**Ana María** "**Anne** " **Hidalgo Aleu** (French: [[an
idalɡo]](/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"), Spanish:
[[iˈðalɣo]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); born 19 June
1959)[2][3] is a Spanish-born French politician who has served as [Mayor of
Paris](/wiki/Mayor_of_Paris "Mayor of Paris") since 2014, the first woman to
hold the office. She is a member of the [Socialist
Party](/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\) "Socialist Party \(France\)") (PS).

Hidalgo was First Deputy Mayor of Paris under Mayor [Bertrand
Delanoë](/wiki/Bertrand_Delano%C3%AB "Bertrand Delanoë") (2001–2014), having
held the title of [Councillor of Paris](/wiki/Council_of_Paris "Council of
Paris") since [2001](/wiki/2001_French_municipal_elections "2001 French
municipal elections").[4] She was elected to the mayorship in
[2014](/wiki/2014_Paris_municipal_election "2014 Paris municipal election")
after Delanoë announced he would not seek a third term. During her first term
as Mayor of Paris she launched the city-wide _Réinventer Paris_ ("Reinvent
Paris") programme,[5] which aimed at refurbishing and allocating obsolescent
sites new uses, as well as opened a [participatory
budgeting](/wiki/Participatory_budgeting "Participatory budgeting") platform
for projects throughout the city.[6] 2015 was marked by instances of [Islamic
terrorism](/wiki/Islamic_terrorism "Islamic terrorism"): the [January _Charlie
Hebdo_ shooting](/wiki/Charlie_Hebdo_shooting "Charlie Hebdo shooting") and
[November coordinated attacks](/wiki/November_2015_Paris_attacks "November
2015 Paris attacks"), including the [Bataclan
theatre](/wiki/Bataclan_\(theatre\) "Bataclan \(theatre\)") massacre, the
aftermath of which she witnessed first-hand.[7]

Her popularity declined following several instances of alleged mismanagement,
to the point that polls showed a majority of voters did not want her to win a
second term in [2020](/wiki/2020_Paris_municipal_election "2020 Paris
municipal election").[8][9] First Deputy Mayor [Bruno
Julliard](/wiki/Bruno_Julliard "Bruno Julliard") resigned in 2018, criticising
Hidalgo's style of governance.[10] In 2019 she oversaw the disaster recovery
efforts for the [Notre-Dame de Paris fire](/wiki/Notre-Dame_de_Paris_fire
"Notre-Dame de Paris fire"). While the [COVID-19
pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_France "COVID-19 pandemic in France") led
to a record low voter turnout, she was reelected with a plurality of the vote.

During her second term as Mayor of Paris, Hidalgo oversaw the city's response
to the COVID-19 pandemic, implementing measures such as nightly curfews,
closure of non-essential shops and the introduction of 50 kilometres (31 mi)
of pop-up cycle lanes known as "_coronapistes_ " to ease pressure on public
transport.[11][12][13] By early 2021, a number of Hidalgo's policies had
gained international attention, such as her proposal to remove over half of
Paris's car parking spaces and turn the [Champs-
Élysées](/wiki/Champs-%C3%89lys%C3%A9es "Champs-Élysées") into a "fantastic
garden".[14][15][16] In 2024, Paris hosted the [Summer
Olympics](/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"); the [opening
ceremony](/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony "2024 Summer Olympics
opening ceremony") was held outside of a stadium for the first time in modern
history, with the athletes [paraded by boat](/wiki/Boat_parade "Boat parade")
along the [Seine](/wiki/Seine "Seine").

On 12 September 2021, Hidalgo announced her candidacy in the [2022
presidential election](/wiki/2022_French_presidential_election "2022 French
presidential election"), despite her 2020 pledge to serve a full second term
as Mayor of Paris.[17][18] She came tenth out of twelve candidates, with 1.75%
of the vote, the lowest result ever for a Socialist candidate in a French
presidential election.

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section:
Early life and education")]

### Family background and youth

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section:
Family background and youth")]

Hidalgo was born in [San Fernando](/wiki/San_Fernando,_C%C3%A1diz "San
Fernando, Cádiz"), [province of Cádiz](/wiki/Province_of_C%C3%A1diz "Province
of Cádiz"), Spain.[1] Her paternal grandfather was a Spanish
[Socialist](/wiki/Spanish_Socialist_Workers_Party "Spanish Socialist Workers
Party") who became a refugee in France after the end of the [Spanish Civil
War](/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War") along with his wife and his
four children. However, her grandparents returned to Spain some time later.
Her grandmother died on the return trip, whereas her grandfather was
[sentenced to death](/wiki/Sentenced_to_death "Sentenced to death"), although
this sentence was eventually commuted to a [life sentence](/wiki/Life_sentence
"Life sentence").

Hidalgo's father, Antonio Hidalgo (born in [Antequera](/wiki/Antequera
"Antequera")),[19] was raised by his maternal grandparents.[_[citation
needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He was
an electrician.[1] In the late 1950s, he married a seamstress named Maria;[1]
they had two daughters, Ana (Anne) and María (Marie). However, due to the
social and economic problems in Spain resulting from the implementation of the
[Stabilization Plan](/wiki/Stabilization_Plan "Stabilization Plan"), Hidalgo's
parents migrated to France in 1961, this time as economic
immigrants.[20][21][22] They settled in [Lyon](/wiki/Lyon "Lyon")[23] with
their two daughters.

Hidalgo grew up in [Vaise](/wiki/Vaise "Vaise"), the [9th arrondissement of
Lyon](/wiki/9th_arrondissement_of_Lyon "9th arrondissement of Lyon"),[24]
speaking Spanish with her parents and French with her sister. Her parents are
now back in Spain[22] while her elder sister, Marie, manages a company in [Los
Angeles](/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). Hidalgo and her parents were
naturalised French when she was fourteen. In 2003, she regained Spanish
nationality and since then has dual French–Spanish citizenship.

### Studies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section:
Studies")]

Hidalgo graduated with a [master's degree](/wiki/Master%27s_degree "Master's
degree") in [social law](/wiki/Social_law "Social law") at [Jean Moulin
University Lyon 3](/wiki/Jean_Moulin_University_Lyon_3 "Jean Moulin University
Lyon 3")[25][26] before completing a [Master of Advanced
Studies](/wiki/Master_of_Advanced_Studies#France_and_francophone_countries
"Master of Advanced Studies") (_DEA_) in social and trade unionism at [Paris
West University Nanterre La
Défense](/wiki/Paris_West_University_Nanterre_La_D%C3%A9fense "Paris West
University Nanterre La Défense").

## Labour inspector

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section:
Labour inspector")]

In 1982, Hidalgo entered the national contest for the _[Inspection du
travail](/wiki/Inspection_du_travail "Inspection du travail")_ (Labour
Inspectorate), ranking fifth. She obtained her first inspector assignment in
[Chevilly-Larue](/wiki/Chevilly-Larue "Chevilly-Larue") in 1984 at the age of
24, before receiving a post in the [15th arrondissement of
Paris](/wiki/15th_arrondissement_of_Paris "15th arrondissement of Paris")
where she lived, a few months later.

In 1991, Hidalgo was appointed director of the National Institute of Labour.
In 1993, she joined the vocational training delegation at the Ministry of
Labour and then obtained a mission at the [International Labour
Office](/wiki/International_Labour_Office "International Labour Office") in
Geneva from 1995 to 1996. She then worked for one year as a project manager
for the Director of Human Resources at the Ministry of Labour. From 1996 to
1997, she was an officer at the Human Resources Directorate of [Compagnie
Générale des Eaux](/wiki/Compagnie_G%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_des_Eaux "Compagnie
Générale des Eaux") (then [Vivendi](/wiki/Vivendi "Vivendi") and Vivendi
Universal).

Hidalgo retired from the [civil service](/wiki/Civil_service "Civil service")
on 1 July 2011, aged 52.[27]

## Member of ministerial cabinets

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section:
Member of ministerial cabinets")]

Between 1997 and 2002, Hidalgo worked as a staffer in three [ministerial
offices](/wiki/Government_of_France#Ministries "Government of France") within
the government of [Lionel Jospin](/wiki/Lionel_Jospin "Lionel Jospin"): first
in the office of [Martine Aubry](/wiki/Martine_Aubry "Martine Aubry") at the
Ministry of Employment and Solidarity as technical advisor; then with [Nicole
Péry](/wiki/Nicole_P%C3%A9ry "Nicole Péry"), Secretary of State for Women's
Rights and Vocational Training, from 1998 to 2000, as technical advisor then
consultant to the firm, participating, in particular, in the drafting of laws
on parity and professional equality between women and men; and from November
2000 to May 2002, as a technical adviser and then mission manager, responsible
for social relations and the status of civil servants, in the office of
[Marylise Lebranchu](/wiki/Marylise_Lebranchu "Marylise Lebranchu"), Minister
of Justice.

Hidalgo said on 4 April 2013, on [RMC](/wiki/RMC_\(France\) "RMC \(France\)"):
"I earn 5,000 euros net per month for my mandates". According to the website
_[Atlantico](/wiki/Atlantico "Atlantico")_ , she received, for all her
revenues, around 8,200 euros net per month.

## Political career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section:
Political career")]

In the [2001 municipal elections](/wiki/2001_French_municipal_elections "2001
French municipal elections"), she led the list of the [Socialist
Party](/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\) "Socialist Party \(France\)") (PS) in
the 15th arrondissement of Paris, which won 26.5% of votes in the first round;
at the second round it then placed behind the list gathered around [Édouard
Balladur](/wiki/%C3%89douard_Balladur "Édouard Balladur") and
[Mayor](/wiki/Mayor_\(France\) "Mayor \(France\)") René Galy-Dejean. She
joined the Council of Paris and was appointed First Deputy Mayor of Paris.

In June 2002, she was a candidate in the [legislative
election](/wiki/2002_French_legislative_election "2002 French legislative
election") in the [12th arrondissement of
Paris](/wiki/12th_arrondissement_of_Paris "12th arrondissement of Paris"),
winning 29.6% of votes in the first round, but Balladur was elected with 54.2%
of the vote. In March 2004, she was elected to the [Regional
Council](/wiki/Regional_council_\(France\) "Regional council \(France\)") of
[Île-de-France](/wiki/%C3%8Ele-de-France "Île-de-France") on the list led by
[Jean-Paul Huchon](/wiki/Jean-Paul_Huchon "Jean-Paul Huchon").

As part of the internal campaign for the nomination of the Socialist candidate
in 2006, she publicly supported [Dominique Strauss-
Kahn](/wiki/Dominique_Strauss-Kahn "Dominique Strauss-Kahn"), while remaining
close to [Lionel Jospin](/wiki/Lionel_Jospin "Lionel Jospin") and [Bertrand
Delanoë](/wiki/Bertrand_Delano%C3%AB "Bertrand Delanoë"). With other female
leaders of the Socialist Party, she criticized the "peoplelisation" of
politics, referring to the promotion of [Ségolène
Royal](/wiki/S%C3%A9gol%C3%A8ne_Royal "Ségolène Royal") as a popularist
widely-identifiable member of the Socialist Party, rather than a classical
Marxist.

In June 2007, she was a candidate at the [legislative
election](/wiki/2007_French_legislative_election "2007 French legislative
election") in the [13th arrondissement of
Paris](/wiki/13th_arrondissement_of_Paris "13th arrondissement of Paris") and
had in the first round 28.2%, against 36.6% for the
[UMP](/wiki/Union_for_a_Popular_Movement "Union for a Popular Movement")
candidate [Jean-François Lamour](/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_Lamour "Jean-
François Lamour"); she was beaten on the second round with 56.7% for Lamour.

### First Deputy Mayor of Paris

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section:
First Deputy Mayor of Paris")]

In 2001, Hidalgo was elected councillor in the 15th arrondissement. She also
joined the Council of Paris, where the left had a majority for the first time
since 1977.

The new Mayor of Paris, [Bertrand Delanoë](/wiki/Bertrand_Delano%C3%AB
"Bertrand Delanoë"), wishing to apply parity within his administration and
among his deputies, appointed Hidalgo as the first deputy responsible for
gender equality and the time office. Close to [François
Hollande](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande"), she thus obtained
her first executive position. In 2002, she acted as Mayor of Paris during the
convalescence of Delanoë after he was stabbed during an attempted
assassination.[28] She confided at the same time to consider a candidacy for
[Mayor of Toulouse](/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Toulouse "List of mayors of
Toulouse") in 2008.

In June 2002, as a candidate in the legislative election in [Paris's 12th
constituency](/wiki/Paris%27s_12th_constituency "Paris's 12th constituency"),
Hidalgo won 29.6% of the vote in the first and only round against 54.2% of the
vote for incumbent [Édouard Balladur](/wiki/%C3%89douard_Balladur "Édouard
Balladur"), who was reelected. She also failed to take [Paris's 13th
constituency](/wiki/Paris%27s_13th_constituency "Paris's 13th constituency")
away from the UMP in June 2007, obtaining 28.2% of the vote in the first
round, then 43.3% of the votes in the second round against 56.7% for the
former Sports Minister [Jean-François Lamour](/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_Lamour
"Jean-François Lamour") (UMP).

In the municipal elections of 9 and 16 March 2008, the assembly list (PS-PCF-
PRG-MRC) that Hidalgo led in the 15th arrondissement of Paris came first in
the first round with 35.9% of the vote (28 313 votes) against a strongly
divided right, 33.9% to [Philippe Goujon](/wiki/Philippe_Goujon "Philippe
Goujon")'s UMP list and 10.1% to [Gérard
d'Aboville](/wiki/G%C3%A9rard_d%27Aboville "Gérard d'Aboville")'s list
(various right). In the second round, her list obtained 47.35% of the votes
against 52.65% obtained by Philippe Goujon, whose list merged with that of
Gérard d'Aboville. Anne Hidalgo remained first Deputy Mayor under Bertrand
Delanoë. She was then responsible for town planning and architecture and seats
for the board of directors of the Parisian Urban Planning Workshop.

In 2017, an article from _[Capital](/wiki/Capital_\(French_magazine\) "Capital
\(French magazine\)")_ stated that Hidalgo had been paid €100,000 by the
Ministry of Labour from 2001 to 2003, while being Bertrand Delanoë's first
deputy. Hidalgo's office indicated that she would file a complaint for
defamation.

### Regional councillor of Île-de-France

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section:
Regional councillor of Île-de-France")]

In the [2004 regional elections](/wiki/2004_French_regional_elections "2004
French regional elections"), Hidalgo was elected to the [Regional Council of
Île-de-France](/wiki/Regional_Council_of_%C3%8Ele-de-France "Regional Council
of Île-de-France") after being voted for Paris on the list conducted at the
regional level by [Jean-Paul Huchon](/wiki/Jean-Paul_Huchon "Jean-Paul
Huchon"). She became a member of the Committee on Transport and Traffic and is
the Chair of the Regional AIDS Information and Prevention Centre (CRIPS).

In the [2010 regional elections](/wiki/2010_French_regional_elections "2010
French regional elections"), the Socialist list she led in Paris came in
second place in the first round, with 26.3% of the vote, behind the list led
by [Chantal Jouanno](/wiki/Chantal_Jouanno "Chantal Jouanno") (28.9%) and in
front of the Green list of Robert Lion (20.6%). In the second round, his list
took the lead with 57.9% of the votes cast, winning in the 1st and 5th
districts, two bastions traditionally anchored on the right. Reelected as
regional councillor, she joined the Committee on Culture and became president
of Île-de-France Europe, which represents the region at the European Union
institutions in [Brussels](/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"). Jean-Luc Romero
succeeded her to the presidency of the CRIPS. Upon her election as Mayor of
Paris, she stepped down as a regional councillor.

### Mayor of Paris

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section:
Mayor of Paris")]

In 2012 Hidalgo announced her intention to seek the succession of Bertrand
Delanoë in the [2014 Paris municipal
election](/wiki/2014_Paris_municipal_election "2014 Paris municipal
election"). The only candidate of her party after the withdrawal of [Jean-
Marie Le Guen](/wiki/Jean-Marie_Le_Guen "Jean-Marie Le Guen"), Hidalgo was
appointed on 22 May 2013 to lead the municipal campaign, with 98.3% of the
votes of 2,715 Paris Socialists. She appointed [Pascal
Cherki](/wiki/Pascal_Cherki "Pascal Cherki") as spokesman for her campaign,
assisted by [Bruno Julliard](/wiki/Bruno_Julliard "Bruno Julliard"), [Rémi
Féraud](/wiki/R%C3%A9mi_F%C3%A9raud "Rémi Féraud") (also co-director of the
campaign with Jean-Louis Missika), [Ian Brossat](/wiki/Ian_Brossat "Ian
Brossat") (after the PS-PCF agreement), [Colombe
Brossel](/wiki/Colombe_Brossel "Colombe Brossel"), [Seybah
Dagoma](/wiki/Seybah_Dagoma "Seybah Dagoma") and [Myriam El
Khomri](/wiki/Myriam_El_Khomri "Myriam El Khomri"). On 10 October 2013, she
was reelected as head of the PS list in the 15th arrondissement.

On 30 March 2014, in the second round, the list she led won a majority in the
Paris Council. In the 15th arrondissement, her list was however defeated by
outgoing Mayor [Philippe Goujon](/wiki/Philippe_Goujon "Philippe Goujon")
(UMP), whose list received 63.4% of the vote in the second round. For the
first time, a candidate thus accessed the mayorship of Paris without being in
the majority in their district. On 5 April 2014, she was elected to the
mayorship by the Paris Council, becoming the first woman to hold the position.
Paris being also a [department](/wiki/Departments_of_France "Departments of
France"), she also became President of the Departmental Council of Paris, one
of ten women (out of 101).

Hidalgo was elected First Vice President of the [Métropole du Grand
Paris](/wiki/Grand_Paris "Grand Paris") on 22 January 2016, _ex officio_ to
her mayoral position.

Ahead of the Socialist Party's [2017
primaries](/wiki/2017_French_Socialist_Party_presidential_primary "2017 French
Socialist Party presidential primary"), Hidalgo endorsed [Vincent
Peillon](/wiki/Vincent_Peillon "Vincent Peillon") as the party's candidate for
the [presidential election](/wiki/2017_French_presidential_election "2017
French presidential election") later that year.[29]

In 2017, [United Nations Secretary
General](/wiki/United_Nations_Secretary_General "United Nations Secretary
General") [António Guterres](/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Guterres "António Guterres")
appointed Hidalgo to the eight-member Independent Panel to Assess, Enhance
Effectiveness of the [United Nations Human Settlements
Programme](/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Settlements_Programme "United Nations
Human Settlements Programme") (UN-Habitat).[30]

On 28 June 2020, Hidalgo was reelected as mayor of Paris, winning 48.5% of
ballots cast.[31] There was a record low voter turnout in the second round of
the municipal elections (64%) which were postponed because of the [COVID-19
pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_France "COVID-19 pandemic in
France").[32] Hidalgo's campaign focused on turning Paris into a 15-minute
city (_Ville Du Quart D'Heure)_ ,[31] aiming to make neighbourhoods more self-
sufficient within each _arrondissement_ in Paris having its own grocery
stores, parks, cafes, sports facilities, health centres, schools and offices
accessible by way of a short walk or bike ride.[33] In December 2020, Hidalgo
received a €90,000 fine (approximately $103,000) from the national government,
after she named 11 women out of 16 in her upper management, which was a
violation of a rule of the French Civil Service Ministry allowing a maximum of
60% of one gender in leadership positions.[34]

### 2022 presidential election

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section:
2022 presidential election")]

In October 2021, Hidalgo took 72% of the votes in the Socialist primary for
the [2022 French presidential
election](/wiki/2022_French_presidential_election "2022 French presidential
election"), ahead of the mayor of [Le Mans](/wiki/Le_Mans "Le Mans"),
[Stéphane Le Foll](/wiki/St%C3%A9phane_Le_Foll "Stéphane Le Foll").[35] At the
start of the following year, she was one of seven names in the [2022 French
People's Primary](/wiki/2022_French_People%27s_Primary "2022 French People's
Primary") for a common left-wing candidate; she was one of three candidates
who did not consent to be on its ballot. She came fifth out of seven
candidates, the lowest of the five who were professional politicians.[36] In
the actual election, she came tenth of 12 candidates with 1.75% of the vote;
she subsequently endorsed [Emmanuel Macron](/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel
Macron") ahead of [Marine Le Pen](/wiki/Marine_Le_Pen "Marine Le Pen").[37]

In 2024, Hidalgo announced that she would not seek a third term as Mayor of
Paris, naming [Rémi Féraud](/wiki/R%C3%A9mi_F%C3%A9raud "Rémi Féraud") as her
preferred successor.[38]

## Political views

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section:
Political views")]

### DADVSI

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section:
DADVSI")]

On 21 December 2005, in the debates on [DADVSI](/wiki/DADVSI "DADVSI") (a
French copyright reform bill), she took a public stand against the amendments
of the Socialist Group introducing the "global licence" to download online
material. On 26 December, she signed with Christophe Girard, [Deputy
Mayor](/wiki/Deputy_Mayor "Deputy Mayor") of Paris responsible for Culture, a
view published in the newspaper _[Le Monde](/wiki/Le_Monde "Le Monde")_
defending her position on behalf of [cultural
diversity](/wiki/Cultural_diversity "Cultural diversity") which would be
threatened by the "global licence."[39] Some
people[_[who?](/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions
"Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] contend that she was in fact
defending the interests of [Vivendi](/wiki/Vivendi "Vivendi") Universal, the
music and film company which employed her a few years earlier.

On 3 January 2006, she presented with François Adibi and the Socialist Party's
Culture Section a report and new recommendations "for a fair solution",
rejecting both the [digital rights management](/wiki/Digital_rights_management
"Digital rights management") (DRM) and the "global licence". She was later
ostracised by the PS leadership which chose to defend in the [National
Assembly](/wiki/National_Assembly_of_France "National Assembly of France") the
"global licence" advocated by [Patrick Bloche](/wiki/Patrick_Bloche "Patrick
Bloche") (Paris), [Didier Mathus](/wiki/Didier_Mathus "Didier Mathus")
([Saône-et-Loire](/wiki/Sa%C3%B4ne-et-Loire "Saône-et-Loire")) and [Christian
Paul](/wiki/Christian_Paul_\(politician\) "Christian Paul \(politician\)")
([Nièvre](/wiki/Ni%C3%A8vre "Nièvre")).

### Anti-cult campaign

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section:
Anti-cult campaign")]

In 2005, Hidalgo took a stand in the debate on [cults](/wiki/Cult "Cult") in
France, becoming the president of a committee of vigilance against the cults
at the [Council of Paris](/wiki/Council_of_Paris "Council of Paris"). She was
especially opposed to the [Church of Scientology](/wiki/Church_of_Scientology
"Church of Scientology") and [New Acropolis](/wiki/New_Acropolis "New
Acropolis"), and participated in a demonstration in front of the Church of
Scientology's premises.[40][41] A map of cults in Paris, created by the Mairie
de Paris at that time and promoted by Hidalgo, was controversial[42] and
Hidalgo filed a complaint against an unknown person for circulating a leaflet
on the Internet signed by a "committee to support Anne Hidalgo", which
requested denunciation of "non-compliant behaviours."[41] Hidalgo denies any
link with this supposed support committee. A complaint that she brought
against the head of the organization that circulated the leaflet was later
dismissed.[43]

### Environmental issues

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section:
Environmental issues")]

See also: [Paris Breathes](/wiki/Paris_Breathes "Paris Breathes")

From May 2016, in order to combat air pollution in the city, Hidalgo oversaw
the introduction of a scheme called "[_Paris Respire_](/wiki/Paris_Breathes
"Paris Breathes")" (literally "Paris Breathes"), which included banning all
cars from certain areas of Paris on the first Sunday of the month, as well as
making public transport and the city's bicycle and electric vehicle schemes
free for the day.[44][45] She also worked further to reduce car usage, with an
increase in the price of parking meters, a ban on free parking on certain
days, and the conversion of certain sections of a highway along the [River
Seine](/wiki/Seine "Seine") into a riverside park.[46] On 24 June 2017, she
joined President [Emmanuel Macron](/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron") in
calling for the adoption of a [Global Pact for the
Environment](/wiki/Global_Pact_for_the_Environment "Global Pact for the
Environment") along with other public figures such as [Laurent
Fabius](/wiki/Laurent_Fabius "Laurent Fabius"), [Nicolas
Hulot](/wiki/Nicolas_Hulot "Nicolas Hulot"), [Arnold
Schwarzenegger](/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger "Arnold Schwarzenegger") and [Ban
Ki-moon](/wiki/Ban_Ki-moon "Ban Ki-moon").[47]

She has also proposed a ban on [diesel motors](/wiki/Diesel_motor "Diesel
motor") in Paris streets[48] and has promised a 24/7 service for the [Paris
Métro](/wiki/Paris_M%C3%A9tro "Paris Métro").[49] Hidalgo aimed to have more
than 970 km (600 mi) of [bike lanes in Paris](/wiki/Cycling_in_Paris "Cycling
in Paris") by 2020.[50]

In February 2020, Hidalgo launched her Paris Mayor reelection campaign with a
focus on making Paris into a [15-minute city](/wiki/15-minute_city "15-minute
city") (_ville du quart d'heure),_ a concept of urban proximity coined by
[Carlos Moreno](/wiki/Carlos_Moreno_\(scientist\) "Carlos Moreno
\(scientist\)"). The name 15-minute city refers to the idea that in cities,
residents of each neighbourhood should be able to reach all necessary
amenities (such as schools, offices, shops, parks, health centres) by a
15-minute walk or bike ride, moving away from car dependency in order to cut
air pollution levels.[51]

In an interview given to _[Le Parisien](/wiki/Le_Parisien "Le Parisien")_ in
October 2020, Hidalgo announced "we must forget about crossing Paris from east
to west by car".[52][53] Hidalgo announced her intention to create permanent
curb-protected cycle lanes and expand the number of "coronapistes", cycle
lanes created during the [COVID-19 pandemic in
France](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_France "COVID-19 pandemic in France").[52]
She also intends to remove over half of the parking spaces in Paris by the end
of her four-year term in office (70,000 out of 140,000 total).[54]

In January 2021, Hidalgo announced that she had approved a €250 million
renovation of the [Champs-Élysées](/wiki/Champs-%C3%89lys%C3%A9es "Champs-
Élysées"), with the intention of reducing space allocated to vehicles by half,
turning roads into green and pedestrianised areas and planting tunnels of
trees to improve air quality.[55]

### Housing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section:
Housing")]

At the start of her first term, Hidalgo stated in an interview that housing is
her number one priority.[56] Under Hidalgo's mayorship, Paris has produced
7,000 social housing units a year since Hidalgo took office, up from 5,000 a
year under her predecessor. She aims for Paris to be 30% social housing by
2030.[57]

### Social media

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section:
Social media")]

In November 2023, Hidalgo publicly quit the social media platform
[X](/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), describing it as a "gigantic global sewer" that
is "destroying our democracies" by spreading abuse and misinformation. Her
move has been seen as a response to the perceived degradation of the platform
since the [acquisition of Twitter by Elon
Musk](/wiki/Acquisition_of_Twitter_by_Elon_Musk "Acquisition of Twitter by
Elon Musk") but has also been linked to attacks on the platform resulting from
the TahitiGate controversy.[58]

### Foreign issues

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section:
Foreign issues")]

She took part in the [March for the Republic and Against
Antisemitism](/wiki/March_for_the_Republic_and_Against_Antisemitism "March for
the Republic and Against Antisemitism") in Paris on 12 November 2023 in
response to the [rise in antisemitism](/wiki/Antisemitism_in_France
"Antisemitism in France") since the beginning of the [Gaza war](/wiki/Gaza_war
"Gaza war").[59]

Hidalgo rejected [calls to ban Israeli athletes from the Summer
Olympics](/wiki/Concerns_and_controversies_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics#Inclusion_of_nations_involved_in_wars
"Concerns and controversies at the 2024 Summer Olympics") because of
[Israel](/wiki/Israel "Israel")'s actions in the [Gaza Strip](/wiki/Gaza_Strip
"Gaza Strip"), saying, "Sanctioning Israel in relation to the Olympic and
Paralympic Games is out of the question because Israel is a democracy."[60]
She called for a ban on all Russian and Belarusian athletes from the Summer
Olympics because of Russia's [invasion of
Ukraine](/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine").[61]

In March 2024, Hidalgo announced that she will not attend the [UN Climate
Change Conference](/wiki/2024_United_Nations_Climate_Change_Conference "2024
United Nations Climate Change Conference") (COP29) in [Baku](/wiki/Baku
"Baku"), [Azerbaijan](/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan"), citing the involvement
of the Azerbaijani government in the [ethnic cleansing of
Armenians](/wiki/Flight_of_Nagorno-Karabakh_Armenians "Flight of Nagorno-
Karabakh Armenians") in the disputed [Nagorno-Karabakh](/wiki/Nagorno-Karabakh
"Nagorno-Karabakh") region in September 2023.[62]

### 2024 Olympics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section:
2024 Olympics")]

Mayor Hidalgo was one of the main faces behind the organization of the [2024
Paris Olympics](/wiki/2024_Paris_Olympics "2024 Paris Olympics"). In a bid to
demonstrate the Seine River would be clean and safe for Olympics events, she
told French radio on 10 July 2024 that she would swim in the river the
following week.[63] She fulfilled her promise a week later on Wednesday, 17
July and swam in the Seine River in a wetsuit.[64] Despite her promotional
efforts, eleven days later Olympic organizers were forced to cancel a training
session for triathletes due to high levels of fecal matter and E-coli bacteria
in the river. Though the competition did take place as scheduled, several
athletes later fell ill with gastrointestinal infections.[65]

## Criticism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section:
Criticism")]

In 2023, Hidalgo faced criticism of her trip to [French
Polynesia](/wiki/French_Polynesia "French Polynesia"), which her political
opponents described as a "holiday". In response, she published a list of
meetings she attended and although she did not visit the [2024 Summer
Olympics](/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") surfing site in
Tahiti, she said her deputy in charge of sports did.[66]

## Personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Anne_Hidalgo&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section:
Personal life")]

Since June 2004, Hidalgo has been married to politician [Jean-Marc
Germain](/wiki/Jean-Marc_Germain_\(politician\) "Jean-Marc Germain
\(politician\)"), whom she met when they both worked in the office of [Martine
Aubry](/wiki/Martine_Aubry "Martine Aubry"), then Minister of Labour. Hidalgo
and Germain reside in the [15th arrondissement of
Paris](/wiki/15th_arrondissement_of_Paris "15th arrondissement of Paris").
They have a child together, Arthur Germain, who is the youngest Frenchman to
swim the [English Channel](/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel").[67][1]

Hidalgo is also the mother of two children – Matthieu, born in 1986, a lawyer,
and Elsa, born in 1988, an engineer – with her ex-husband Philippe Jantet.[68]

Hidalgo had a [Catholic](/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") education but is today an
outspoken [atheist](/wiki/Atheist "Atheist").[69][70][71]

**Olivier Faure** ([[ɔlivje fɔʁ]](/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")
[](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/de/Olivier_Faure.ogg/Olivier_Faure.ogg.mp3
"Play audio")[ⓘ](/wiki/File:Olivier_Faure.ogg "File:Olivier Faure.ogg"); born
18 August 1968) is a French politician who has served as the [First
Secretary](/wiki/First_Secretary_of_the_French_Socialist_Party "First
Secretary of the French Socialist Party") of the [Socialist
Party](/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\) "Socialist Party \(France\)") since
2018 and [Member of the National Assembly](/wiki/Deputy_\(France\) "Deputy
\(France\)") for [Seine-et-Marne's 11th constituency](/wiki/Seine-et-
Marne%27s_11th_constituency "Seine-et-Marne's 11th constituency") since 2012.
He was elected to the post of first secretary in the party's [Aubervilliers
Congress](/wiki/Aubervilliers_Congress "Aubervilliers Congress") and re-
elected in the 2021 Villeurbanne Congress. Faure was previously the head of
the [New Left group](/wiki/New_Left_group "New Left group") (French: _Groupe
Nouvelle Gauche_), the parliamentary group formed around the PS in the
[National Assembly](/wiki/National_Assembly_\(France\) "National Assembly
\(France\)"), from December 2016 to April 2018.[1]

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Olivier_Faure&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section:
Early life")]

Olivier Faure was born in 1968 to a Vietnamese nurse of Chinese origin and a
French tax agent of Spanish origin.[2] After spending his early childhood in
[Réunion](/wiki/R%C3%A9union "Réunion"), he grew up in [Metropolitan
France](/wiki/Metropolitan_France "Metropolitan France"), where he pursued his
studies. Faure attended the [Lycée](/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e "Lycée") Pothier in
Orléans and then the [University of Orléans](/wiki/University_of_Orl%C3%A9ans
"University of Orléans"), where he graduated with a [Master of Advanced
Studies](/wiki/Master_of_Advanced_Studies "Master of Advanced Studies") (MAS)
in [economic law](/wiki/Economic_law "Economic law"), and the [Paris 1
Panthéon-Sorbonne University](/wiki/Paris_1_Panth%C3%A9on-Sorbonne_University
"Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University"), where he graduated with a MAS in
[political science](/wiki/Political_science "Political science").[3]

## Political career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Olivier_Faure&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section:
Political career")]

Faure joined the [Socialist Party](/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\) "Socialist
Party \(France\)") (PS) at the age of 16 and also became an activist for the
[National Union of Students of
France](/wiki/Union_Nationale_des_%C3%89tudiants_de_France "Union Nationale
des Étudiants de France") (UNEF). It was as a member of the PS that he met
[Benoît Hamon](/wiki/Beno%C3%AEt_Hamon "Benoît Hamon"), with whom he shared an
apartment for a time.[4] In 1991, at the age of 23, Faure became the
secretary-general of the Young Rocardiens, a group supporting Prime Minister
[Michel Rocard](/wiki/Michel_Rocard "Michel Rocard").[2]

From 1991 to 1993, Faure worked with Gérard Gouzes, the president of the
commission of law in the [National
Assembly](/wiki/National_Assembly_\(France\) "National Assembly \(France\)").
From 1993 to 1997, Faure served as the chief executive of a business with 150
employees.[5][6] Faure then served as an advisor to [Martine
Aubry](/wiki/Martine_Aubry "Martine Aubry") in the Ministry of Labour,
Employment and Vocational Training from 1997 to 2000 and assistant cabinet
director to Socialist First Secretary [François
Hollande](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande") from 2000 to 2007.
At the beginning of 2007, he published a comic book titled _Ségo, François,
papa et moi_ about the inner workings of [Ségolène
Royal](/wiki/S%C3%A9gol%C3%A8ne_Royal "Ségolène Royal")'s campaign to become
the PS candidate in the [2007 French presidential
election](/wiki/2007_French_presidential_election "2007 French presidential
election").[7]

Faure ran to represent [Seine-et-Marne's 8th constituency](/wiki/Seine-et-
Marne%27s_8th_constituency "Seine-et-Marne's 8th constituency") in the
National Assembly in the [2007 French legislative
elections](/wiki/2007_French_legislative_election "2007 French legislative
election") but lost to [Chantal Brunel](/wiki/Chantal_Brunel "Chantal Brunel")
of the [Union for a Popular Movement](/wiki/Union_for_a_Popular_Movement
"Union for a Popular Movement") (UMP).[7] In October 2007, Faure joined the
leader of the Socialist group in the National Assembly, [Jean-Marc
Ayrault](/wiki/Jean-Marc_Ayrault "Jean-Marc Ayrault"), to become the
formation's secretary-general.[2]

### Member of the National Assembly, 2012–present

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Olivier_Faure&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section:
Member of the National Assembly, 2012–present")]

During the [2011 Socialist presidential
primary](/wiki/2011_French_Socialist_Party_presidential_primary "2011 French
Socialist Party presidential primary"), Faure worked as the chief of
communications for the François Hollande campaign.[8] After Hollande won the
primary, Faure became his "expert opinion" in the [2012 French presidential
election](/wiki/2012_French_presidential_election "2012 French presidential
election").[9] The Socialist candidate went on to win the general election,
and Faure was appointed special adviser to Prime Minister [Jean-Marc
Ayrault](/wiki/Jean-Marc_Ayrault "Jean-Marc Ayrault"), from which position he
resigned soon after.

In January 2012, Faure was nominated by the PS as its candidate in [Seine-et-
Marne's 11th constituency](/wiki/Seine-et-Marne%27s_11th_constituency "Seine-
et-Marne's 11th constituency") for the [2012 French legislative
elections](/wiki/2012_French_legislative_election "2012 French legislative
election"). The party was well-positioned to win the constituency due to an
electoral pact with [Europe Ecology – The
Greens](/wiki/Europe_Ecology_%E2%80%93_The_Greens "Europe Ecology – The
Greens") (EELV), who withdrew their candidate, [Jean-Marc Brûlé](/wiki/Jean-
Marc_Br%C3%BBl%C3%A9 "Jean-Marc Brûlé"), from the race.[10] Faure was elected
on 17 June with 63.2% of the vote in the second round, against the UMP's Cathy
Bissonier with 36.78% of the vote.[11] Upon entering the National Assembly, he
was named third vice-president of the [Socialist, Republican and
Citizen](/wiki/Socialist_group,_associated_\(National_Assembly\) "Socialist
group, associated \(National Assembly\)") (SRC) group of deputies. On 18 July
2012, Faure became the national secretary of communications for the PS,
thereby joining the party's executive team.[12]

On 15 April 2014, Faure was chosen as one of the spokespeople for the PS at
the party's national council.[13] In June 2014, Faure introduced an
[amendment](/wiki/Amendment "Amendment") adding a tax of two euros per person
per night stayed in the [Île-de-France](/wiki/%C3%8Ele-de-France "Île-de-
France") "for financing _francilien_ public transit."[14] During this session
of the National Assembly, he served as the special rapporteur for the
collective and rail transport infrastructure budget. In December 2014, Faure
successfully passed an amendment to the law on finances, implementing a
[Navigo card](/wiki/Navigo_card "Navigo card") with a single price.

On 13 December 2016, Faure succeeded [Bruno Le Roux](/wiki/Bruno_Le_Roux
"Bruno Le Roux") to become the head of the [Socialist, Republican and
Citizen](/wiki/Socialist_group,_associated_\(National_Assembly\) "Socialist
group, associated \(National Assembly\)") group.[15] His election by 137 votes
against 120 for [Guillaume
Bachelay](/w/index.php?title=Guillaume_Bachelay&action=edit&redlink=1
"Guillaume Bachelay \(page does not exist\)") was regarded as a blow to Prime
Minister [Manuel Valls](/wiki/Manuel_Valls "Manuel Valls"). Faure and Valls
had become opponents after the Prime Minister refused to consider Faure's
compromise amendment to Article 2 of the [El Khomri law](/wiki/El_Khomri_law
"El Khomri law") in July 2016.[16] As president of the SRC group, Faure
attempted to find new compromises on the El Khomri law and legislation
concerning the [revocation of French citizenship](/wiki/Denaturalization
"Denaturalization").[4]

In 2016, Faure considered endorsing [Emmanuel Macron](/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron
"Emmanuel Macron") in the [2017 French presidential
election](/wiki/2017_French_presidential_election "2017 French presidential
election"), but ultimately refused to support him after a meeting between the
two.[17] Faure was re-elected to the National Assembly in the [2017 French
legislative elections](/wiki/2017_French_legislative_election "2017 French
legislative election") with EELV's Paulin Roy as his designated substitute,
receiving 61.1% of the vote against [La République En
Marche](/wiki/La_R%C3%A9publique_En_Marche! "La République En Marche!")'s
(LREM) Amandine Rubinelli.[18] On 22 June 2017, he was re-elected to the
presidency of the Socialist group with 28 votes against 3 votes for [Delphine
Batho](/wiki/Delphine_Batho "Delphine Batho").

Faure abstained in a July 2017 vote of confidence in the government of Prime
Minister [Édouard Philippe](/wiki/%C3%89douard_Philippe "Édouard
Philippe").[19] He also notably delivered speeches on the ordinances of the
[El Khomri law](/wiki/El_Khomri_law "El Khomri law") and the counter-budget on
a bill of finances.[20] In April 2018, _[Les
Jours](/w/index.php?title=Les_Jours&action=edit&redlink=1 "Les Jours \(page
does not exist\)")_ wrote that "with 27.2% of his votes in line with En
Marche, Olivier Faure is not part of the deputies most hostile to the
parliamentary majority's policies."[21]

After Faure was elected as First Secretary of the Socialist Party in March
2018, [Valérie Rabault](/wiki/Val%C3%A9rie_Rabault "Valérie Rabault") replaced
him as the president of the New Left group.

### First Secretary of the Socialist Party

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Olivier_Faure&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section:
First Secretary of the Socialist Party")]

In January 2018, Faure announced his candidacy for the position of First
Secretary of the Socialist Party in view of the upcoming [Aubervilliers
Congress](/wiki/Aubervilliers_Congress "Aubervilliers Congress"). He was the
first signatory of the motion "Socialists, the path of the renaissance" and
was notably supported by [Martine Aubry](/wiki/Martine_Aubry "Martine Aubry"),
the mayor of [Lille](/wiki/Lille "Lille"), and [Carole
Delga](/wiki/Carole_Delga "Carole Delga"), the president of the region of
[Occitania](/wiki/Occitania_\(administrative_region\) "Occitania
\(administrative region\)"). A [Harris
Interactive](/wiki/Harris_Insights_%26_Analytics "Harris Insights &
Analytics") poll among PS supporters placed him in second place, far behind
former minister [Stéphane Le Foll](/wiki/St%C3%A9phane_Le_Foll "Stéphane Le
Foll"), who benefited from greater publicity due to his governmental
responsibilities under the Hollande presidency.[22] Faure came first in the
first round of the election for first secretary on 15 March 2018, receiving
48.37% of the vote against 26.45% for [Stéphane Le
Foll](/wiki/St%C3%A9phane_Le_Foll "Stéphane Le Foll").[23] The latter then
withdrew from the race, making Faure the presumptive first secretary.[24]
Faure then won the election with 86% of the vote on 29 March.[25][26] He was
inaugurated as first secretary in the Aubrevilliers Congress on 7
April.[27][28] On 15 April, Faure proposed new leadership for the PS' national
council, with [Corinne Narassiguin](/wiki/Corinne_Narassiguin "Corinne
Narassiguin") being duly chosen as the new national secretary for coordination
and means as well as [Boris Vallaud](/wiki/Boris_Vallaud "Boris Vallaud") and
Gabrielle Siry becoming the new spokespeople.[29]

Over the course of 2019, Faure was speculated to harbour ambitions for the
presidency in the [2022 French presidential
elections](/wiki/2022_French_presidential_election "2022 French presidential
election"), which he denied.[30] During the [2019 European Parliament election
in France](/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_France "2019 European
Parliament election in France"), several polls projected that the alliance
between PS and [Raphaël Glucksmann](/wiki/Rapha%C3%ABl_Glucksmann "Raphaël
Glucksmann")'s [Place Publique](/wiki/Place_Publique "Place Publique") would
receive less than 5% of the vote. The alliance's joint electoral list
ultimately won 6.2% of the vote and six seats, including three Socialists,
while the list of [Benoît Hamon](/wiki/Beno%C3%AEt_Hamon "Benoît Hamon"), who
had left the PS, won 3.3%. Faure supported [unions of the
left](/wiki/Union_of_the_Left_\(France\) "Union of the Left \(France\)") and
environmentalists, a strategy that was considered effective after the PS
gained control of several large cities in the [2020 French municipal
elections](/wiki/2020_French_municipal_elections "2020 French municipal
elections") by joining alliances in the first and second rounds.[31][32]
During the [Villeurbanne](/wiki/Villeurbanne "Villeurbanne") Congress in
September 2021, Faure was re-elected as first secretary with 73.49% of the
vote against 26.52% for [Hélène Geoffroy](/wiki/H%C3%A9l%C3%A8ne_Geoffroy
"Hélène Geoffroy").[33]

After the PS suffered a historic defeat in the presidential election, Faure
proposed discussing cooperation between the PS and [La France
Insoumise](/wiki/La_France_Insoumise "La France Insoumise") (LFI) for the
[2022 French legislative election](/wiki/2022_French_legislative_election
"2022 French legislative election"), a possibility that divided his party.[34]
Faure's position was ultimately adopted by the party's National Office, which
also rejected Carole Delga's proposals against cooperation. This triggered the
departure of several PS executives. At the beginning of May 2022, while
negotiations were under way between LFI and the PS for the June legislative
elections, 1,000 local and national party executives challenged Faure on a
potential electoral pact between the two parties. They denounced the proposal
as a "surrender", citing disagreements with the LFI's plans to "disobey
certain European rules", leave [NATO](/wiki/NATO "NATO"), abandon nuclear
energy, and dismantle [EPRs](/wiki/EPR_\(nuclear_reactor\) "EPR \(nuclear
reactor\)").[35]

In the [2024 parliamentary election](/wiki/2024_French_legislative_election
"2024 French legislative election"), the Socialist Party more than doubled its
seats in the [National Assembly](/wiki/National_Assembly_\(France\) "National
Assembly \(France\)") as part of the left-wing [NFP](/wiki/New_Popular_Front
"New Popular Front") alliance. In December 2024, NFP, together with far-right
[National Rally](/wiki/National_Rally "National Rally") ousted Prime Minister
[Michel Barnier](/wiki/Michel_Barnier "Michel Barnier") in a motion of
censure.[36] PS decided not to support another motion of censure against
[Francois Bayrou](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Bayrou "François Bayrou") in February
2025, initiated by [La France Insoumise](/wiki/La_France_Insoumise "La France
Insoumise"), in exchange for concessions in new budget. Votes of PS deputies
weren't needed to escape the motion of censure. Concessions included
renegotiation of [2023 pension
reform](/wiki/2023_French_pension_reform_strikes "2023 French pension reform
strikes"), abandonment of the 4000 job cuts in education, 500 jub cuts in
[France Travail](/wiki/France_Travail "France Travail") and overseas budget
cuts, one billion euro increase in healthcare spending and the "maintenance"
of the new "differential contribution on high incomes".[37][38] This decision
was sharply criticised by LFI, [Jean-Luc Mélenchon](/wiki/Jean-
Luc_M%C3%A9lenchon "Jean-Luc Mélenchon") reacted: "The NFP is reduced by one
party".[39]

## Personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Olivier_Faure&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section:
Personal life")]

Faure is married to Soria Blatmann, who was as a member of the presidential
cabinet of [Emmanuel Macron](/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron") in the
field of human rights until February 2018, when she went to work with the new
director-general of [UNESCO](/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO"), [Audrey
Azoulay](/wiki/Audrey_Azoulay "Audrey Azoulay").[40] Faure was also formerly
close to [Christophe Castaner](/wiki/Christophe_Castaner "Christophe
Castaner"), with whom he broke off relations after Castaner became the
[Minister of the Interior](/wiki/Minister_of_the_Interior_\(France\) "Minister
of the Interior \(France\)") in the LREM majority government.[41] In February
2020, Castaner claimed that he had accompanied Faure "in his divorces and
separations," a statement that provoked indignation from the first
secretary.[42]

## Political positions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Olivier_Faure&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section:
Political positions")]

As a deputy under the presidency of François Hollande, Faure opposed the
government's proposed constitutional revisions to extend the revocation of
French citizenship.[43] He also opposed the Socialist "frondeur" rebels and
supported the adoption of the [El Khomri law](/wiki/El_Khomri_law "El Khomri
law") without resorting to [article 49.3 of the
Constitution](/wiki/Article_49_of_the_French_Constitution "Article 49 of the
French Constitution") while attempting to unite his parliamentary group on
this compromise, which was opposed by Manuel Valls.[44]

Faure participated in a Paris rally of police officers in May 2021, where he
denounced how police were "constantly exposed to aggression" and demanded that
they have a "right of inspection" on judicial decisions. This proposal was
criticized by several figures on the left, who accused it of violating the
principle of [separation of powers](/wiki/Separation_of_powers "Separation of
powers").[45][46] Faure then clarified his argument and walked back his use of
the expression "right of inspection," calling it "unfortunate".[47]

In January 2022, Faure supported and successfully passed a resolution
condemning the [Uyghur genocide](/wiki/Persecution_of_Uyghurs_in_China
"Persecution of Uyghurs in China") in China.[48]
